Reference: Araujo, Costa and Sant'Anna (2026)

Model Setting

The paper estimates the carbon-efficient forest cover of the Brazilian Amazon, defined as the land use that would arise if farmers fully internalized the social cost of the carbon stored in each plot of forest. It builds a dynamic discrete choice model in which profit-maximizing agents choose every year whether each field is used for crops, pasture or forest, subject to conversion costs and with forward-looking option values. The model is estimated on a panel of land use for more than 5.7 billion 30-m pixels in each year 2008-2017 (MapBiomas), combined with potential yields (FAO GAEZ), crop prices at regional trade hubs (ESALQ), newly computed transportation costs to export ports, and a 30-m map of aboveground biomass (Zarin et al. 2016). The sample is pixels outside protected areas that were not deforested before 2000. Estimation follows Scott (2013): the CCP structure and one-period finite dependence deliver an Euler-type equation that is a linear regression with transition probabilities on the left-hand side, so the value function never has to be solved during estimation.

The setting motivates three features. First, deforestation is driven by pasture: between 2008 and 2017, 90% of the deforested area became pasture for extensive cattle ranching, and 7% of 2008 forest became pasture by 2017 versus only 1% that became cropland. Second, deforestation is not a one-way street: 13% of 2008 pasture had reverted to forest by 2017, so the model allows regeneration. Third, both private returns (yields, transport costs) and social damages (carbon density) vary sharply over space, so the conservation trade-off is local and policies that ignore this heterogeneity are inefficient. The key counterfactuals compare the business-as-usual (BAU) steady state with the efficient one under a social cost of carbon of 50 US dollars per ton of CO2_22​, and evaluate a carbon tax (equivalently, a carbon-based payment for ecosystem services) and excise taxes on cattle and crops.

Fields, Land Uses and Payoffs

The decision unit is a field iii (a 30-m pixel), grouped into locations mmm (1-km cells). Each field is run by a rational agent who is the residual claimant of its cash flow, whether as formal owner, tenant or informal holder. In every year t=1,2,…,∞t=1,2,\ldots,\inftyt=1,2,…,∞ the agent chooses a land use j∈J={crop,pasture,forest}j\in J=\{\text{crop},\text{pasture},\text{forest}\}j∈J={crop,pasture,forest}, where forest means leaving the land unused under native vegetation. The flow profit is separable:

πj(wmt,εimjt)=rj(wmt;α)+εimjt(9.5.4.1)\pi_j(w_{mt},\varepsilon_{imjt})=r_j(w_{mt};\alpha)+\varepsilon_{imjt} \tag{9.5.4.1}πj​(wmt​,εimjt​)=rj​(wmt​;α)+εimjt​(9.5.4.1)

where wmt∈RLw_{mt}\in\mathbb{R}^Lwmt​∈RL is a vector of location-specific state variables (prices, land characteristics, transport costs, and unobservables), rj(⋅;α)r_j(\cdot;\alpha)rj​(⋅;α) is known up to the parameter vector α\alphaα, and εimjt\varepsilon_{imjt}εimjt​ is a field-, choice- and time-specific shock. Changing land use from last period's use kkk to current use jjj entails a conversion cost Φjk(wmt;φ)\Phi_{jk}(w_{mt};\varphi)Φjk​(wmt​;φ), which enters the payoff with a positive sign (so a cost is a negative value). Three assumptions discipline the problem: (1) wmtw_{mt}wmt​ follows a Markov process unaffected by field-level decisions, F(wm,t+1∣wmt,εimjt,j)=F(wm,t+1∣wmt)F(w_{m,t+1}\mid w_{mt},\varepsilon_{imjt},j)=F(w_{m,t+1}\mid w_{mt})F(wm,t+1​∣wmt​,εimjt​,j)=F(wm,t+1​∣wmt​), consistent with price-taking farmers; (2) εimjt\varepsilon_{imjt}εimjt​ is i.i.d. type-I extreme value across time and choices; (3) there is no cost of keeping the same use, Φjj=0\Phi_{jj}=0Φjj​=0.

Dynamic Problem and Choice Probabilities

An agent who used the field for kkk in t−1t-1t−1 solves:

V(k,wmt,εimt)=max⁡j∈J{Φjk(wmt;φ)+rj(wmt;α)+εimjt+ρE[Vˉ(j,wm,t+1)∣wmt]}(9.5.4.2)V(k,w_{mt},\varepsilon_{imt})=\max_{j\in J}\left\{\Phi_{jk}(w_{mt};\varphi)+r_j(w_{mt};\alpha)+\varepsilon_{imjt}+\rho E\left[\bar{V}(j,w_{m,t+1})\mid w_{mt}\right]\right\} \tag{9.5.4.2}V(k,wmt​,εimt​)=j∈Jmax​{Φjk​(wmt​;φ)+rj​(wmt​;α)+εimjt​+ρE[Vˉ(j,wm,t+1​)∣wmt​]}(9.5.4.2)

where Vˉ(j,wmt)=Eε[V(j,wmt,εimt)]\bar{V}(j,w_{mt})=E_{\varepsilon}[V(j,w_{mt},\varepsilon_{imt})]Vˉ(j,wmt​)=Eε​[V(j,wmt​,εimt​)] is the integrated value function, εimt∈R3\varepsilon_{imt}\in\mathbb{R}^3εimt​∈R3 stacks the three shocks, and ρ\rhoρ is the discount factor. The continuation value contains the option value of future land uses: for example, clearing forest for pasture today lowers the cost of converting to crops tomorrow. The non-random part of the payoff is the choice-specific value function:

υ(j,k,wmt)=Φjk(wmt;φ)+rj(wmt;α)+ρE[Vˉ(j,wm,t+1)∣wmt](9.5.4.3)\upsilon(j,k,w_{mt})=\Phi_{jk}(w_{mt};\varphi)+r_j(w_{mt};\alpha)+\rho E\left[\bar{V}(j,w_{m,t+1})\mid w_{mt}\right] \tag{9.5.4.3}υ(j,k,wmt​)=Φjk​(wmt​;φ)+rj​(wmt​;α)+ρE[Vˉ(j,wm,t+1​)∣wmt​](9.5.4.3)

so that V(k,wmt,εimt)=max⁡j{υ(j,k,wmt)+εimjt}V(k,w_{mt},\varepsilon_{imt})=\max_{j}\{\upsilon(j,k,w_{mt})+\varepsilon_{imjt}\}V(k,wmt​,εimt​)=maxj​{υ(j,k,wmt​)+εimjt​}. The extreme value assumption yields logit conditional choice probabilities (CCPs), i.e. the probability that a field transitions from kkk to jjj:

p(j∣k,wmt)=exp⁡(υ(j,k,wmt))∑j′∈Jexp⁡(υ(j′,k,wmt)),k,j∈J(9.5.4.4)p(j\mid k,w_{mt})=\frac{\exp\left(\upsilon(j,k,w_{mt})\right)}{\sum_{j'\in J}\exp\left(\upsilon(j',k,w_{mt})\right)},\qquad k,j\in J \tag{9.5.4.4}p(j∣k,wmt​)=∑j′∈J​exp(υ(j′,k,wmt​))exp(υ(j,k,wmt​))​,k,j∈J(9.5.4.4)

and hence the Hotz and Miller (1993) inversion:

log⁡(p(j∣k,wmt)p(j′∣k,wmt))=υ(j,k,wmt)−υ(j′,k,wmt),k,j,j′∈J(9.5.4.5)\log\left(\frac{p(j\mid k,w_{mt})}{p(j'\mid k,w_{mt})}\right)=\upsilon(j,k,w_{mt})-\upsilon(j',k,w_{mt}),\qquad k,j,j'\in J \tag{9.5.4.5}log(p(j′∣k,wmt​)p(j∣k,wmt​)​)=υ(j,k,wmt​)−υ(j′,k,wmt​),k,j,j′∈J(9.5.4.5)

Euler-Type Equation

The model has the one-period finite dependence property: if jjj is chosen in t+1t+1t+1, it does not matter for t+2t+2t+2 onward whether jjj or kkk was chosen in ttt. Compare two paths starting from kkk: (a) switch to jjj in ttt and stay in jjj in t+1t+1t+1; (b) stay in kkk in ttt and switch to jjj in t+1t+1t+1. Both reach the same state in t+1t+1t+1, so their continuation values from t+2t+2t+2 cancel. Using the Hotz-Miller inversion for the choices in ttt and t+1t+1t+1 and Φjj=0\Phi_{jj}=0Φjj​=0:

log⁡(p(j∣k,wmt)p(k∣k,wmt))−ρlog⁡(p(j∣k,wm,t+1)p(j∣j,wm,t+1))=Φjk(wmt;φ)−ρ Φjk(wm,t+1;φ)+rj(wmt;α)−rk(wmt;α)+ηjV(wmt)−ηkV(wmt),j,k∈J(9.5.4.6)\begin{aligned} \log\left(\frac{p(j\mid k,w_{mt})}{p(k\mid k,w_{mt})}\right)-\rho\log\left(\frac{p(j\mid k,w_{m,t+1})}{p(j\mid j,w_{m,t+1})}\right) &=\Phi_{jk}(w_{mt};\varphi)-\rho\,\Phi_{jk}(w_{m,t+1};\varphi)+r_j(w_{mt};\alpha)\\ &\quad-r_k(w_{mt};\alpha)+\eta_j^V(w_{mt})-\eta_k^V(w_{mt}),\qquad j,k\in J \end{aligned} \tag{9.5.4.6}log(p(k∣k,wmt​)p(j∣k,wmt​)​)−ρlog(p(j∣j,wm,t+1​)p(j∣k,wm,t+1​)​)​=Φjk​(wmt​;φ)−ρΦjk​(wm,t+1​;φ)+rj​(wmt​;α)−rk​(wmt​;α)+ηjV​(wmt​)−ηkV​(wmt​),j,k∈J​(9.5.4.6)

where ηjV(wmt)=ρ(E[Vˉ(j,wm,t+1)∣wmt]−Vˉ(j,wm,t+1))\eta_j^V(w_{mt})=\rho(E[\bar{V}(j,w_{m,t+1})\mid w_{mt}]-\bar{V}(j,w_{m,t+1}))ηjV​(wmt​)=ρ(E[Vˉ(j,wm,t+1​)∣wmt​]−Vˉ(j,wm,t+1​)) is the expectational error in continuation values. Under rational expectations this error has mean zero conditional on information at ttt. The left-hand side contains only CCPs observable in the data; the right-hand side contains primitives. The state is split into observables and unobservables, wmt=(xmt,ξmt)w_{mt}=(x_{mt},\xi_{mt})wmt​=(xmt​,ξmt​), with xmt∈RL−3x_{mt}\in\mathbb{R}^{L-3}xmt​∈RL−3 and a vector of choice-specific unobserved shocks ξmt∈R3\xi_{mt}\in\mathbb{R}^3ξmt​∈R3. Flow returns are linear in parameters with an additive unobservable:

rj(wmt;α)=αˉj+αj′Rj(xmt)+ξjmt,j∈J(9.5.4.7)r_j(w_{mt};\alpha)=\bar{\alpha}_j+\alpha_j'R_j(x_{mt})+\xi_{jmt},\qquad j\in J \tag{9.5.4.7}rj​(wmt​;α)=αˉj​+αj′​Rj​(xmt​)+ξjmt​,j∈J(9.5.4.7)

Conversion costs have a fixed transition-specific part, and clearing forest may depend on the location's carbon stock:

Φjk(wmt;φ)=φˉjk+φ 1{k=forest} hm(9.5.4.8)\Phi_{jk}(w_{mt};\varphi)=\bar{\varphi}_{jk}+\varphi\,\mathbb{1}\{k=\text{forest}\}\,h_m \tag{9.5.4.8}Φjk​(wmt​;φ)=φˉ​jk​+φ1{k=forest}hm​(9.5.4.8)

where hmh_mhm​ is the time-invariant potential carbon stock of location mmm.

Flow Profits

Crop. The crop grown on each pixel is not observed, so crop returns use a weighted average of the main crops c∈Cc\in Cc∈C (soy and maize) in the location's mesoregion, with weights scms_{cm}scm​ from the 2006 Agricultural Census:

r~mt=∑c∈Cscm(pct−zmc)ymc(9.5.4.9)\tilde{r}_{mt}=\sum_{c\in C}s_{cm}\left(p_{ct}-z_{mc}\right)y_{mc} \tag{9.5.4.9}r~mt​=c∈C∑​scm​(pct​−zmc​)ymc​(9.5.4.9)

where ymcy_{mc}ymc​ is the potential yield, pctp_{ct}pct​ the price at destination markets, and zmcz_{mc}zmc​ the transport cost to the nearest export port. The crop payoff is:

rcrop(wmt;α)=αcropr~mt+αˉcrop+ξcrop,m,t(9.5.4.10)r_{\text{crop}}(w_{mt};\alpha)=\alpha_{\text{crop}}\tilde{r}_{mt}+\bar{\alpha}_{\text{crop}}+\xi_{\text{crop},m,t} \tag{9.5.4.10}rcrop​(wmt​;α)=αcrop​r~mt​+αˉcrop​+ξcrop,m,t​(9.5.4.10)

Because r~mt\tilde{r}_{mt}r~mt​ is the only regressor measured in money (reais), αcrop\alpha_{\text{crop}}αcrop​ is used to monetize everything else. The term αˉcrop+ξcrop,m,t\bar{\alpha}_{\text{crop}}+\xi_{\text{crop},m,t}αˉcrop​+ξcrop,m,t​ absorbs input, wage and other costs, and ξcrop,m,t\xi_{\text{crop},m,t}ξcrop,m,t​ may be correlated with yields and transport costs (roads may follow good land).

Pasture. Cattle raising has time-to-build dynamics and no pixel-level herd data, so the pasture return is modeled flexibly through the FAO pasture suitability index, interacted with year-specific coefficients and with road distance to port:

rj(wmt;α)=αj,t1ym,j+αj2dmym,j+αˉj+ξj,m,t,j=pasture(9.5.4.11)r_j(w_{mt};\alpha)=\alpha_{j,t}^1y_{m,j}+\alpha_j^2d_my_{m,j}+\bar{\alpha}_j+\xi_{j,m,t},\qquad j=\text{pasture} \tag{9.5.4.11}rj​(wmt​;α)=αj,t1​ym,j​+αj2​dm​ym,j​+αˉj​+ξj,m,t​,j=pasture(9.5.4.11)

The time-varying coefficient αpasture,t1\alpha_{\text{pasture},t}^1αpasture,t1​ absorbs unmodeled cattle-market dynamics such as beef price formation.

Forest. The return of leaving the field unused depends on its carbon stock:

rforest(wmt;α)=αforesthm+ξforest,m,t(9.5.4.12)r_{\text{forest}}(w_{mt};\alpha)=\alpha_{\text{forest}}h_m+\xi_{\text{forest},m,t} \tag{9.5.4.12}rforest​(wmt​;α)=αforest​hm​+ξforest,m,t​(9.5.4.12)

with αˉforest\bar{\alpha}_{\text{forest}}αˉforest​ normalized to zero. The coefficient αforest\alpha_{\text{forest}}αforest​ is the farmer's perceived value of forest carbon: it combines environmental enforcement tied to forest density (how far policy already makes farmers internalize the standing forest) and private costs and benefits of dense forest (encroachment risk on blurred property boundaries; protection of springs, riparian forest and soil).

Structural Regression

Substituting the payoff specifications into the Euler-type equation gives the estimating equation, for j,k∈Jj,k\in Jj,k∈J:

log⁡(p(j∣k,wmt)p(k∣k,wmt))−ρlog⁡(p(j∣k,wm,t+1)p(j∣j,wm,t+1))=(1−ρ)φˉjk+(1−ρ)φ 1{k=forest}hm+αj′Rj(xmt)−αk′Rk(xmt)+αˉj−αˉk+ξjmt−ξkmt+ηjV(wmt)−ηkV(wmt)(9.5.4.13)\begin{aligned} \log\left(\frac{p(j\mid k,w_{mt})}{p(k\mid k,w_{mt})}\right)-\rho\log\left(\frac{p(j\mid k,w_{m,t+1})}{p(j\mid j,w_{m,t+1})}\right) &=(1-\rho)\bar{\varphi}_{jk}+(1-\rho)\varphi\,\mathbb{1}\{k=\text{forest}\}h_m+\alpha_j'R_j(x_{mt})-\alpha_k'R_k(x_{mt})\\ &\quad+\bar{\alpha}_j-\bar{\alpha}_k+\xi_{jmt}-\xi_{kmt}+\eta_j^V(w_{mt})-\eta_k^V(w_{mt}) \end{aligned} \tag{9.5.4.13}log(p(k∣k,wmt​)p(j∣k,wmt​)​)−ρlog(p(j∣j,wm,t+1​)p(j∣k,wm,t+1​)​)​=(1−ρ)φˉ​jk​+(1−ρ)φ1{k=forest}hm​+αj′​Rj​(xmt​)−αk′​Rk​(xmt​)+αˉj​−αˉk​+ξjmt​−ξkmt​+ηjV​(wmt​)−ηkV​(wmt​)​(9.5.4.13)

The intercepts αˉj\bar{\alpha}_jαˉj​ absorb choice-specific components constant across space and time, so ξjmt\xi_{jmt}ξjmt​ has mean zero (an innocuous normalization). To separate fixed conversion costs from choice constants, a grounding condition is imposed: regeneration is passive (land left idle), so φˉforest,k=0\bar{\varphi}_{\text{forest},k}=0φˉ​forest,k​=0 for k∈{crop,pasture}k\in\{\text{crop},\text{pasture}\}k∈{crop,pasture}. The six transition-specific intercepts then satisfy:

τj,k=(1−ρ)φˉjk+αˉj−αˉk,j≠k(9.5.4.14)\tau_{j,k}=(1-\rho)\bar{\varphi}_{jk}+\bar{\alpha}_j-\bar{\alpha}_k,\qquad j\neq k \tag{9.5.4.14}τj,k​=(1−ρ)φˉ​jk​+αˉj​−αˉk​,j=k(9.5.4.14)

With αˉforest=0\bar{\alpha}_{\text{forest}}=0αˉforest​=0, this leaves four φˉjk\bar{\varphi}_{jk}φˉ​jk​ and two αˉj\bar{\alpha}_jαˉj​, which are exactly identified.

Data and CCP Construction

MapBiomas classifies every 30-m pixel each year; uses are aggregated to crop, pasture, forest and other (other and protected areas are dropped). For each pair of years and each transition, a 0/1 matrix marks pixels making the transition and is averaged up to 1-km locations, at which suitability (ymcy_{mc}ymc​, ym,pasturey_{m,\text{pasture}}ym,pasture​), transport (zmcz_{mc}zmc​, dmd_mdm​), carbon (hmh_mhm​) and the shocks ξjmt\xi_{jmt}ξjmt​ are homogeneous. Many 1-km cells still have near-zero transition rates, which break the Hotz-Miller inversion, so CCPs are smoothed with a Gaussian filter (standard deviation 150 km) over latitude and longitude. Biomass is converted to potential CO2_22​ release (divide by 2 for carbon, multiply by 44/12), and all carbon is assumed released on clearing (slash and burn, fast decomposition). Transport costs are estimated by regressing ESALQ freight costs on quality-adjusted road distances by nonlinear least squares, as in Donaldson (2018), then adding waterways and computing least-cost bimodal routes to the nearest port with Dijkstra's algorithm; dmd_mdm​ is the quality-adjusted distance before monetization. The discount factor is fixed at ρ=0.9\rho=0.9ρ=0.9 (a 10% annual rate), since it is poorly identified.

Estimation and Identification

Estimation has two steps; inference uses a block bootstrap with 1,000 iterations on a 25 km by 25 km grid, allowing spatial dependence in ξjmt\xi_{jmt}ξjmt​. There are 79,478,568 observations.

Step 1: within-location estimation. First-differencing the structural regression removes the fixed location component of ξjmt\xi_{jmt}ξjmt​ (distance to the forest core, technology, access to electricity, etc.), as well as all time-invariant terms (hmh_mhm​, conversion costs, forest return):

ΔYj,k,m,t=αcropXj,k,m,t+(αpasture,t1−αpasture,t−11)Wj,k,m,t+Δζj,k,m,t(9.5.4.15)\Delta Y_{j,k,m,t}=\alpha_{\text{crop}}X_{j,k,m,t}+\left(\alpha_{\text{pasture},t}^1-\alpha_{\text{pasture},t-1}^1\right)W_{j,k,m,t}+\Delta\zeta_{j,k,m,t} \tag{9.5.4.15}ΔYj,k,m,t​=αcrop​Xj,k,m,t​+(αpasture,t1​−αpasture,t−11​)Wj,k,m,t​+Δζj,k,m,t​(9.5.4.15)

where ΔYj,k,m,t\Delta Y_{j,k,m,t}ΔYj,k,m,t​ is the first difference of the left-hand side of the structural regression, and the differenced crop and pasture returns are:

Xj,k,m,t={r~mt−r~m,t−1if j=crop, k≠crop−(r~mt−r~m,t−1)if k=crop, j≠crop0otherwiseWj,k,m,t={ym,pastureif j=pasture, k≠pasture−ym,pastureif k=pasture, j≠pasture0otherwise(9.5.4.16)X_{j,k,m,t}=\begin{cases} \tilde{r}_{mt}-\tilde{r}_{m,t-1} & \text{if } j=\text{crop},\ k\neq\text{crop}\\ -(\tilde{r}_{mt}-\tilde{r}_{m,t-1}) & \text{if } k=\text{crop},\ j\neq\text{crop}\\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\qquad W_{j,k,m,t}=\begin{cases} y_{m,\text{pasture}} & \text{if } j=\text{pasture},\ k\neq\text{pasture}\\ -y_{m,\text{pasture}} & \text{if } k=\text{pasture},\ j\neq\text{pasture}\\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \tag{9.5.4.16}Xj,k,m,t​=⎩⎨⎧​r~mt​−r~m,t−1​−(r~mt​−r~m,t−1​)0​if j=crop, k=cropif k=crop, j=cropotherwise​Wj,k,m,t​=⎩⎨⎧​ym,pasture​−ym,pasture​0​if j=pasture, k=pastureif k=pasture, j=pastureotherwise​(9.5.4.16)

The error Δζj,k,m,t\Delta\zeta_{j,k,m,t}Δζj,k,m,t​ collects the differences of ηjV−ηkV\eta_j^V-\eta_k^VηjV​−ηkV​ and of ξj,m,t−ξk,m,t\xi_{j,m,t}-\xi_{k,m,t}ξj,m,t​−ξk,m,t​ between ttt and t−1t-1t−1. Differencing creates endogeneity because ηjV(wm,t−1)\eta_j^V(w_{m,t-1})ηjV​(wm,t−1​) is a forecast error correlated with r~mt\tilde{r}_{mt}r~mt​. Following Anderson and Hsiao (1981), the twice-lagged return instruments Xj,k,m,tX_{j,k,m,t}Xj,k,m,t​; it is known at t−1t-1t−1 and hence orthogonal to the expectational error:

E[Δζj,k,m,t r~m,t−2]=0(9.5.4.17)E\left[\Delta\zeta_{j,k,m,t}\,\tilde{r}_{m,t-2}\right]=0 \tag{9.5.4.17}E[Δζj,k,m,t​r~m,t−2​]=0(9.5.4.17)

Identification of αcrop\alpha_{\text{crop}}αcrop​ comes from price changes over time, amplified in the cross-section because r~mt−r~m,t−1=∑cscmymc(pct−pc,t−1)\tilde{r}_{mt}-\tilde{r}_{m,t-1}=\sum_{c}s_{cm}y_{mc}(p_{ct}-p_{c,t-1})r~mt​−r~m,t−1​=∑c​scm​ymc​(pct​−pc,t−1​) scales price changes by local yields and crop shares. The Arellano-Bond estimator would be more efficient but is impractical at this sample size, and efficiency is not a concern.

Step 2: levels. Plugging α^crop\hat{\alpha}_{\text{crop}}α^crop​ and the estimated changes in αpasture,t1\alpha_{\text{pasture},t}^1αpasture,t1​ into the structural regression, the remaining parameters (αforest\alpha_{\text{forest}}αforest​, (1−ρ)φ(1-\rho)\varphi(1−ρ)φ, the pasture coefficients and the intercepts τj,k\tau_{j,k}τj,k​) are estimated by OLS in levels. These level parameters rest on cross-sectional variation across locations.

Key Estimates

  • Crop coefficient: α^crop=0.392\hat{\alpha}_{\text{crop}}=0.392α^crop​=0.392 (s.e. 0.016), so higher crop returns raise conversion to crops. The year-to-year changes in the pasture suitability coefficient range from −0.055-0.055−0.055 to 0.0580.0580.058.

  • Forest carbon: α^forest=4.41\hat{\alpha}_{\text{forest}}=4.41α^forest​=4.41 (0.32), or 11.26 after dividing by αcrop\alpha_{\text{crop}}αcrop​. Given the units (hmh_mhm​ in 10410^4104 t/ha, r~mt\tilde{r}_{mt}r~mt​ in 10310^3103 reais/ha), this implies a perceived value of preserving forest carbon of 1.126 reais per ton of CO2_22​ per year. This is far below annualized social costs of carbon (7.6 reais based on Nordhaus 2014, 20.6 reais based on EPA 2016), so farmers internalize little of the externality. Converted to a present value (divide by 1−ρ=0.11-\rho=0.11−ρ=0.1) at 0.243 US dollars per real, the perceived value is 2.74 US dollars per ton.

  • Conversion costs: the carbon term (1−ρ)φ=−4.18(1-\rho)\varphi=-4.18(1−ρ)φ=−4.18 (or −10.67-10.67−10.67 in money units), so denser forest is costlier to clear: each ton of CO2_22​ raises the clearing cost by 10.67 reais per hectare, about 20% of the forest-to-pasture conversion cost for an average field (300 t/ha). In monetized (1−ρ)(1-\rho)(1−ρ) units, the fixed costs are −1.18-1.18−1.18 (forest to pasture), −2.06-2.06−2.06 (forest to crop), −1.52-1.52−1.52 (pasture to crop) and −0.51-0.51−0.51 (crop to pasture): clearing for crops is costlier than clearing for pasture, consistent with the extra investment needed to prepare cropland. The constants are αˉpasture=0.13\bar{\alpha}_{\text{pasture}}=0.13αˉpasture​=0.13 and αˉcrop=−0.66\bar{\alpha}_{\text{crop}}=-0.66αˉcrop​=−0.66.

Counterfactual Steady States

Counterfactuals require solving the value function. To avoid specifying transitions for prices, all uncertainty in the state is removed by fixing each location at its time average, wm=1T∑twmtw_m=\frac{1}{T}\sum_tw_{mt}wm​=T1​∑t​wmt​, which holds current market conditions fixed. The logit structure gives the integrated Bellman equation:

Carbon and the Efficient Benchmark

The efficient land use sets farmers' perceived value of forest carbon equal to the social cost of carbon of 50 US dollars per ton of CO2_22​, i.e. a carbon tax of 47.26 US dollars on top of the 2.74 already perceived. A carbon tax on non-forest uses based on the potential carbon content of the land is equivalent in this model to a flow of payments for ecosystem services for carbon kept in the forest (or to tighter enforcement); it is implemented by raising the perceived carbon return αforest\alpha_{\text{forest}}αforest​. Excess emissions of BAU over the efficient scenario in location mmm are:

ΔCO2m=(Am(forest,wm⋆)−Am(forest,wm))hm(9.5.4.20)\Delta CO2_m=\left(A_m(\text{forest},w_m^{\star})-A_m(\text{forest},w_m)\right)h_m \tag{9.5.4.20}ΔCO2m​=(Am​(forest,wm⋆​)−Am​(forest,wm​))hm​(9.5.4.20)

where wm⋆w_m^{\star}wm⋆​ is the efficient-policy state, and totals sum over locations. For welfare, the model is extended to value carbon socially. For a policy τ\tauτ, steady-state welfare in location mmm decomposes as:

Wτ(wm)=Vˉτ(wm)+11−ρETAXm−SCC×EΔCO2m(9.5.4.21)W^{\tau}(w_m)=\bar{V}^{\tau}(w_m)+\frac{1}{1-\rho}ETAX_m-SCC\times E\Delta CO2_m \tag{9.5.4.21}Wτ(wm​)=Vˉτ(wm​)+1−ρ1​ETAXm​−SCC×EΔCO2m​(9.5.4.21)

where Vˉτ(wm)\bar{V}^{\tau}(w_m)Vˉτ(wm​) is the private integrated steady-state value (integrated over initial land uses), ETAXmETAX_mETAXm​ the steady-state expected tax payment, SCCSCCSCC the non-internalized social cost of carbon, and EΔCO2mE\Delta CO2_mEΔCO2m​ expected steady-state emissions. Welfare is thus the present value of private profits before taxes minus the social cost of expected deforestation; using gross profits makes the measure invariant to whether the policy is a tax or an equivalent payment scheme.

Counterfactual Results

Price elasticities. A 10% crop price increase gives a long-run cropland elasticity of 6.60, a pasture cross-elasticity of −0.25-0.25−0.25, a forest cover elasticity of −0.42-0.42−0.42 and a carbon-released elasticity of 0.13 (0.5 Gt of extra CO2_22​, 25 billion US dollars of damages). For cattle prices: forest −1.66-1.66−1.66, crop −0.44-0.44−0.44, pasture 1.43, carbon released 1.82, so cattle markets matter much more for forests. With myopic agents (ρ=0\rho=0ρ=0), the forest elasticities fall to −0.14-0.14−0.14 (crop price) and −0.47-0.47−0.47 (cattle price), confirming that static models understate long-run responses.

Efficient versus BAU. The efficient steady state preserves 99.7% of the carbon stock and 97% of the forest cover in the sample, against 51% of the carbon stock under BAU. The efficiency gap is 42 billion tons of CO2_22​ (95% CI 39-45) and 1,186,216 km2^22 of forest (about twice France), with 92% of the emissions gap coming from conversion to pasture. Closing it would require stopping the current deforestation pattern for about four decades. Locally the gap reaches 40,000 tons of CO2_22​ per km2^22 (2 million US dollars of damages per km2^22), mostly along waterways and roads in Para, where carbon density and agricultural profitability are both high; it is small at the low-carbon fringe (Mato Grosso, Tocantins) and in the remote far west. Regeneration matters little on the efficient path (primary forest is conserved) but a lot under BAU, where fields are exhausted and abandoned: ignoring it raises the gap by 42% after 15 years.

Carbon tax. The response is highly convex: a carbon tax of 2.5 US dollars per ton saves 25 billion tons of CO2_22​ and 526 thousand km2^22 (60% of the efficient savings), 5 dollars saves 34 billion tons (81%), and 10 dollars preserves 95% of the efficient carbon stock. Preserving carbon is cheap deep in the forest where carbon and transport costs are high, and land is the main input of extensive ranching, so a small rise in the perceived cost of clearing is a large cost shock. The 10 dollar figure is below the 18.50 dollars of Souza-Rodrigues (2019), reflecting post-PPCDAm enforcement and the dynamic model, but above the 5 dollars per ton paid by the Amazon Fund.

Cattle and crop taxes. An ad valorem tax on cattle ranching returns is a second-best instrument because it is not tied to carbon density. A 20% tax saves about 15.8 billion tons of CO2_22​; matching the 34 billion tons of a 5-dollar carbon tax needs a 60% cattle tax (50% matches its forest cover). Crop taxes barely change emissions, since crops are a small share of land use.

Welfare. Moving from BAU to the efficient path yields welfare gains of about 1.66 trillion US dollars: 2.02 trillion of avoided emission damages minus 356 billion of foregone private profits, more than five dollars of corrective gain per dollar of lost profit. Most gains are captured by carbon taxes below 15 dollars per ton. The welfare-maximizing cattle tax is 100%, which achieves 87% of the first-best gains (about 1.8 trillion of avoided damages, 273 billion of lost profits), because it also distorts land toward crops and taxes pasture even in low-carbon, high-productivity areas.

Extensions and Robustness

  • Tipping points. BAU deforests 57% of the sample; if protected areas stay intact and pre-2000 clearing does not regenerate, total Amazon deforestation reaches 31%, below the 40% dieback threshold. Other externalities (biodiversity, rainfall, tipping points) are omitted, so the gap is a lower bound.

  • Equilibrium effects. With a world beef supply elasticity of 1.43 and demand elasticity of −0.45-0.45−0.45, the efficient land use raises world beef prices by 4.16%, offsetting at most 5.9% of grazing area.

  • Trade. In a partial equilibrium model where Brazilian beef is sold to the EU and the rest of the world, the domestic price response to a change dtdtdt in the EU tariff is approximately:

    dpp≈s ϵDϵS−ϵD dt=−0.06 0.451.43+0.45 dt=−0.014 dt(9.5.4.22)\frac{dp}{p}\approx s\,\frac{\epsilon_D}{\epsilon_S-\epsilon_D}\,dt=-0.06\,\frac{0.45}{1.43+0.45}\,dt=-0.014\,dt \tag{9.5.4.22}pdp​≈sϵS​−ϵD​ϵD​​dt=−0.061.43+0.450.45​dt=−0.014dt(9.5.4.22)

    with an EU export share sss of 6%. Removing a 20% tariff plus 20% non-tariff barriers in an EU-Mercosur deal raises beef prices by 0.6%, cutting forest cover by 1.00% (9,500 km2^22, 0.46 Gt of CO2_22​, 23 billion US dollars of damages).

  • Carbon accounting. If regenerated forest holds zero carbon for 30 years, the BAU-efficient gap rises to 58 billion tons, but a 10-dollar tax still saves 49 billion tons (40 in the baseline). Estimating on pixels deforested before 2008 (secondary vegetation) gives a gap of 1,408,000 km2^22 and 58 billion tons. Excluding peatlands leaves estimates nearly unchanged.

  • Discount factor. With ρ=0.95\rho=0.95ρ=0.95 conversion costs are generally lower, the gap is 53 Gt, and a 10-dollar tax closes 92% of it.

  • Technology. Modeling crop returns with soy-maize double cropping gives a perceived carbon value of 2.86 reais per ton per year and an efficiency gap of 37 billion tons of CO2_22​.

This is the assumed per-period payoff of using field iii in location mmm for land use jjj in year ttt. It has two additive pieces. The first, rj(wmt;α)r_j(w_{mt};\alpha)rj​(wmt​;α), is the deterministic return of use jjj; it depends only on the location-level state wmtw_{mt}wmt​ (prices, yields, transport costs, carbon stock and location-level unobservables), so it is common to all 30-m pixels inside the same 1-km cell. The second, εimjt\varepsilon_{imjt}εimjt​, is an idiosyncratic shock specific to the field, the use and the year, observed by the agent but not by the econometrician.

Additive separability is what makes the model tractable. Combined with the assumption that εimjt\varepsilon_{imjt}εimjt​ is i.i.d. type-I extreme value, it delivers the logit choice probabilities in equation (4) and the log-sum formula in equation (18). Because the shock is the only source of heterogeneity across pixels inside a location, the share of pixels in mmm moving from use kkk to use jjj is a consistent estimate of the choice probability, which is how the data are built.

The scale of the payoff is pinned down by normalizing the variance of εimjt\varepsilon_{imjt}εimjt​ (the standard logit scale normalization), so all payoffs are in units of the shock's standard deviation rather than in money. Money units are recovered later by dividing by αcrop\alpha_{\text{crop}}αcrop​ from equation (10). The conversion cost is not part of πj\pi_jπj​; it enters separately in equation (2) because it depends on last period's use.

This is the Bellman equation of the agent who controls field iii. The endogenous state is the previous land use kkk; the exogenous states are the location vector wmtw_{mt}wmt​ and the vector of current shocks εimt\varepsilon_{imt}εimt​. For each candidate use jjj the agent adds up four terms: the conversion payoff Φjk(wmt;φ)\Phi_{jk}(w_{mt};\varphi)Φjk​(wmt​;φ) (negative when switching is costly, zero when j=kj=kj=k), the deterministic flow return rj(wmt;α)r_j(w_{mt};\alpha)rj​(wmt​;α) and the shock εimjt\varepsilon_{imjt}εimjt​ from equation (1), and the discounted expected continuation value ρE[Vˉ(j,wm,t+1)∣wmt]\rho E[\bar{V}(j,w_{m,t+1})\mid w_{mt}]ρE[Vˉ(j,wm,t+1​)∣wmt​].

Two assumptions shape the continuation term. First, because the shocks are i.i.d. over time, tomorrow's shocks are integrated out and only the integrated value function Vˉ\bar{V}Vˉ appears. Second, because the state wmtw_{mt}wmt​ evolves as a Markov process that individual fields do not affect, the expectation is conditional on wmtw_{mt}wmt​ only and not on the choice. The choice jjj matters for the future only because it becomes tomorrow's endogenous state, the first argument of Vˉ\bar{V}Vˉ.

That dependence is the dynamic content of the model. Today's use changes tomorrow's conversion costs: a field cleared for pasture today can be turned into cropland tomorrow at cost Φcrop,pasture\Phi_{\text{crop},\text{pasture}}Φcrop,pasture​ rather than Φcrop,forest\Phi_{\text{crop},\text{forest}}Φcrop,forest​, and a field kept as forest retains the option to clear later when prices are high. With ρ=0\rho=0ρ=0 the problem collapses to a static logit over Φjk+rj\Phi_{jk}+r_jΦjk​+rj​; the paper shows that this myopic version understates long-run price responses. The deterministic part of the bracket is given a name in equation (3).

This equation defines the choice-specific (conditional) value function: the value of choosing use jjj today on a field previously in use kkk, net of today's shock εimjt\varepsilon_{imjt}εimjt​ and assuming optimal behavior from tomorrow on. It is simply the non-random part of the bracket in equation (2), so that the Bellman equation can be written compactly as

V(k,wmt,εimt)=max⁡j∈J{υ(j,k,wmt)+εimjt}.V(k,w_{mt},\varepsilon_{imt})=\max_{j\in J}\left\{\upsilon(j,k,w_{mt})+\varepsilon_{imjt}\right\}.V(k,wmt​,εimt​)=j∈Jmax​{υ(j,k,wmt​)+εimjt​}.

The previous use kkk enters υ\upsilonυ only through the conversion payoff Φjk\Phi_{jk}Φjk​; the flow return rjr_jrj​ and the continuation value ρE[Vˉ(j,wm,t+1)∣wmt]\rho E[\bar{V}(j,w_{m,t+1})\mid w_{mt}]ρE[Vˉ(j,wm,t+1​)∣wmt​] depend on the chosen use jjj alone. Hence, for two different starting uses kkk and k′k'k′,

υ(j,k,wmt)−υ(j,k′,wmt)=Φjk(wmt;φ)−Φjk′(wmt;φ).\upsilon(j,k,w_{mt})-\upsilon(j,k',w_{mt})=\Phi_{jk}(w_{mt};\varphi)-\Phi_{jk'}(w_{mt};\varphi).υ(j,k,wmt​)−υ(j,k′,wmt​)=Φjk​(wmt​;φ)−Φjk′​(wmt​;φ).

This property is the source of one-period finite dependence used in equation (6): once two fields are in the same use, their histories are irrelevant, so differences in values across histories reduce to differences in conversion costs.

Writing the problem in terms of υ\upsilonυ turns the dynamic problem into a static-looking discrete choice with mean utilities υ(j,k,wmt)\upsilon(j,k,w_{mt})υ(j,k,wmt​), which gives the logit probabilities in equation (4) and the inversion in equation (5).

A second inversion follows from the same formula and is used in the derivation of equation (6). Vˉ(k,wmt)=υ(j,k,wmt)−log⁡p(j∣k,wmt)+γfor any j∈J.\bar{V}(k,w_{mt})=\upsilon(j,k,w_{mt})-\log p(j\mid k,w_{mt})+\gamma\qquad\text{for any } j\in J .Vˉ(k,wmt​)=υ(j,k,wmt​)−logp(j∣k,wmt​)+γfor any j∈J.

This is the parametric form assumed for the deterministic flow return in equation (1). Linearity in parameters matters because, once this form is substituted into the Euler-type equation (6), the estimating equation (13) is a linear regression, so it can be estimated by OLS and linear IV on almost 80 million observations without ever solving the dynamic program. This is the constructed measure of the gross return to cropping one hectare in location mmm in year ttt, in thousand reais per hectare. For each crop ccc in the set CCC (soy and maize), pctp_{ct}pct​ is the price at the destination market, zmcz_{mc}zmc​ the cost of hauling one unit of the crop from mmm to the nearest export port, so pct−zmcp_{ct}-z_{mc}pct​−zmc​ is the farm-gate price; multiplying by the potential yield ymcy_{mc}ymc​ (FAO GAEZ, tons per hectare) gives farm-gate revenue per hectare. The weights scms_{cm}scm​ are the shares of each crop in the mesoregion of mmm from the 2006 Agricultural Census, used because the land-use data do not reveal which crop is grown on a pixel.

The index combines three sources of variation: time variation from prices only, and cross-sectional variation from yields, transport costs and crop shares. Its change over time is

The measure is revenue net of transport only; it leaves out wages, inputs and other costs, which are absorbed by the intercept and the unobservable in equation (10). Using potential rather than realized yields avoids the selection problem that realized yields are observed only where crops are actually grown, and using pre-sample weights keeps the index from responding to the land-use choices being explained.

The coefficient αforest\alpha_{\text{forest}}αforest​ is the key behavioral parameter of the paper, the perceived private value of keeping a unit of carbon standing for one year. It is a reduced form for several forces that scale with forest density: fines and enforcement that are more intense in dense forest, private benefits of forest such as protection of water and soil, and private costs such as encroachment risk. It measures how much of the carbon externality farmers already internalize.

Six equations, six unknowns, a unique solution. The logic is that a round trip, for example forest to crop and back, nets out the intercepts: τc,f+τf,c\tau_{c,f}+\tau_{f,c}τc,f​+τf,c​ is the sum of the two annualized conversion costs, and assuming the return leg is free attributes all of it to clearing. If regeneration were in fact costly, the estimated clearing costs would be overstated in absolute value and the choice constants shifted accordingly.

Evaluating the bracket case by case gives the three branches of equation (16). If the destination is crop and the origin is not, the bracket is +1+1+1: a rise in crop returns makes moving into crops more attractive. If the origin is crop and the destination is not, the bracket is −1-1−1: the same rise makes leaving crops less attractive. If neither end of the transition is crop (forest to pasture, pasture to forest), or if j=k=cropj=k=\text{crop}j=k=crop, the bracket is 000. Why OLS fails. The error Δζj,k,m,t\Delta\zeta_{j,k,m,t}Δζj,k,m,t​ contains −[ηjV(wm,t−1)−ηkV(wm,t−1)]-[\eta_j^V(w_{m,t-1})-\eta_k^V(w_{m,t-1})]−[ηjV​(wm,t−1​)−ηkV​(wm,t−1​)], the forecast error made at t−1t-1t−1 about values realized at ttt. A surprise in crop prices at ttt raises r~mt\tilde{r}_{mt}r~mt​, hence Xj,k,m,tX_{j,k,m,t}Xj,k,m,t​, and at the same time makes realized continuation values differ from their expectation, so the regressor and the error are correlated by construction.

Why the instrument is valid. Under rational expectations each expectational error is mean independent of the information available when the forecast was made: E[ηjV(wm,t−1)∣wm,t−1]=0E[\eta_j^V(w_{m,t-1})\mid w_{m,t-1}]=0E[ηjV​(wm,t−1​)∣wm,t−1​]=0 and E[ηjV(wmt)∣wmt]=0E[\eta_j^V(w_{mt})\mid w_{mt}]=0E[ηjV​(wmt​)∣wmt​]=0. The lagged return r~m,t−2\tilde{r}_{m,t-2}r~m,t−2​ is known at t−1t-1t−1 (and a fortiori at ttt), so it is orthogonal to both. Relevance requires that the lagged level predicts the change r~mt−r~m,t−1\tilde{r}_{mt}-\tilde{r}_{m,t-1}r~mt​−r~m,t−1​, which holds when prices are mean reverting; the paper reports this first stage.

One assumption is left implicit: the condition also requires r~m,t−2\tilde{r}_{m,t-2}r~m,t−2​ to be uncorrelated with the change in unobserved returns, [ξj,m,t−ξk,m,t]−[ξj,m,t−1−ξk,m,t−1][\xi_{j,m,t}-\xi_{k,m,t}]-[\xi_{j,m,t-1}-\xi_{k,m,t-1}][ξj,m,t​−ξk,m,t​]−[ξj,m,t−1​−ξk,m,t−1​]. The rational expectations argument does not deliver this; it holds, for example, if ξj,m,t\xi_{j,m,t}ξj,m,t​ is a location fixed effect plus innovations unrelated to past crop prices. The year-specific pasture terms Wj,k,m,tW_{j,k,m,t}Wj,k,m,t​ are treated as exogenous.

using the change of variables u=e−eu=e^{-e}u=e−e. Hence the mean of the maximum is μ+γ\mu+\gammaμ+γ:

which is equation (18). For each location it is a system of three equations (one per previous use kkk) in the three unknowns Vˉ(k,wm)\bar{V}(k,w_m)Vˉ(k,wm​). The right-hand side is a contraction with modulus ρ\rhoρ in the sup norm, because the log-sum-exp function has partial derivatives equal to the choice probabilities, which sum to one; iterating from any starting guess converges to the unique solution. The solution is plugged into equation (4) to obtain the steady-state transition matrix p(j∣k,wm)p(j\mid k,w_m)p(j∣k,wm​), whose invariant distribution is Am(j,wm)A_m(j,w_m)Am​(j,wm​).

This defines the long-run land-use elasticity reported in the counterfactuals. A(j,w)A(j,w)A(j,w) is the total steady-state area in use jjj when the state of every location is w={wm}mw=\{w_m\}_mw={wm​}m​: for each location one solves equation (18), forms the CCPs of equation (4), computes the invariant distribution Am(j,wm)A_m(j,w_m)Am​(j,wm​) of the resulting three-state Markov chain, and sums over locations. w~\tilde{w}w~ is the same state after a permanent proportional price change of size Δ\DeltaΔ (for instance Δ=0.1\Delta=0.1Δ=0.1 for a 10 percent increase in crop prices in equation (9), or a 10 percent increase in the pasture return of equation (11) for cattle prices).

The formula is an arc elasticity: the percentage change in steady-state area divided by the percentage change in the price. It is computed for a discrete change rather than as a derivative because the steady state has no closed form. For example, the reported forest elasticity of −1.66-1.66−1.66 with respect to cattle prices means that with Δ=0.1\Delta=0.1Δ=0.1

A(forest,w~)−A(forest,w)A(forest,w)=−1.66×0.1=−16.6 percent.\frac{A(\text{forest},\tilde{w})-A(\text{forest},w)}{A(\text{forest},w)}=-1.66\times 0.1=-16.6\ \text{percent}.A(forest,w)A(forest,w~)−A(forest,w)​=−1.66×0.1=−16.6 percent.

Three points of interpretation. It is a long-run concept: it compares two steady states and so includes the full adjustment through conversion costs and option values, unlike a one-year response read off the CCPs. It is a partial-equilibrium concept: prices are changed exogenously and held there. And it may be an own-price elasticity (cropland with respect to crop prices, 6.60) or a cross elasticity (forest with respect to crop prices, −0.42-0.42−0.42), depending on which jjj and which price are used.

This defines the excess carbon emissions of business as usual relative to the efficient allocation in location mmm. Am(forest,wm)A_m(\text{forest},w_m)Am​(forest,wm​) is the steady-state probability that a pixel of mmm is forest under the estimated parameters (BAU), and Am(forest,wm⋆)A_m(\text{forest},w_m^{\star})Am​(forest,wm⋆​) is the same probability when the perceived value of carbon αforest\alpha_{\text{forest}}αforest​ in equation (12) is raised to the social cost of carbon of 50 dollars per ton. Their difference is the share of the location that is forest in the efficient steady state but cleared under BAU; multiplying by the carbon stock hmh_mhm​ (tons of CO2_22​ per hectare of standing forest) and by the area of the location converts it into tons of CO2_22​.

The definition embeds a carbon accounting assumption: a pixel holds its full potential stock hmh_mhm​ when it is forest and zero otherwise, all carbon is released when the forest is cleared, and regenerated forest counts as holding hmh_mhm​ again. The paper relaxes the last part in a robustness exercise in which regrowth holds no carbon for 30 years, which raises the aggregate gap from 42 to 58 billion tons.

Summing over locations gives the aggregate efficiency gap,

ΔCO2=∑mΔCO2m,\Delta CO2=\sum_{m}\Delta CO2_m ,ΔCO2=m∑​ΔCO2m​,

estimated at 42 billion tons. Because the forest-share difference is multiplied by hmh_mhm​, the gap is concentrated where both terms are large: locations with dense forest that are also profitable for agriculture. Remote locations have large hmh_mhm​ but little BAU deforestation, and low-carbon fringe locations are deforested under BAU but contribute little carbon per hectare. The same expression with a different policy state in place of wm⋆w_m^{\star}wm⋆​ gives the emissions saved by any carbon or cattle tax.

The paper derives this decomposition in its Appendix A.2; what follows is a reconstruction of the steady-state accounting behind it. Social welfare in location mmm is defined as the present value of private payoffs gross of tax payments (taxes are a transfer, not a resource cost) minus the social cost of the carbon released that farmers do not already internalize.

Step 1 (private value as a present value). The first two terms depend on behavior only, not on who collects the money: a carbon tax and an equivalent payment for standing forest induce the same choices and the same gross profits, so they give the same WτW^{\tau}Wτ although Vˉτ\bar{V}^{\tau}Vˉτ alone differs between them. The sign is intuitive: a lower tariff (dt<0dt<0dt<0) raises EU demand at any producer price, so the producer price rises, but only slightly because the EU is a small share of sales.
